q13.question_html:
You have an Azure subscription that contains a virtual network named VNet1. VNet1 contains four subnets named:

  • Gateway
  • Perimeter
  • NVA
  • Production

The NVA subnet contains two network virtual appliances (NVAs) that perform network traffic inspection between the Perimeter subnet and the Production subnet.

You need to implement an Azure Load Balancer for the NVAs. The solution must meet the following requirements:

  • The NVAs must run in an active-active configuration that uses automatic failover.
  • The NVAs must load balance traffic to two services on the Production subnet. The services have different IP addresses.

Question

Which three actions should you perform?
q13.explanation_html:
Correct actions: B, C, and E

You need a Standard Load Balancer in front of the NVAs for high availability and advanced features.

B. Deploy a standard load balancer — Correct

  • Basic Load Balancer lacks support for HA Ports, Availability Zones, and certain high-availability scenarios.
  • Standard Load Balancer is required for active-active NVA setups, HA Ports, and better SLA/reliability.

C. Add two load balancing rules that have HA Ports and Floating IP enabled — Correct

  • HA Ports rule (port 0, any protocol) is the standard way to load balance all traffic through NVAs (common for network appliances doing inspection).
  • Floating IP (Direct Server Return) must be enabled so that return traffic from Production services goes back through the same NVA (preserves source IP and symmetric routing).
  • You need two rules because there are two distinct services (different IPs) on the Production subnet.

E. Add a frontend IP configuration, a backend pool, and a health probe — Correct

  • Frontend IP: The IP that receives traffic (typically in the Perimeter subnet).
  • Backend pool: Contains the two NVAs in the NVA subnet.
  • Health probe: Monitors NVA health for automatic failover (active-active with failure detection).

These three actions together satisfy:

  • Active-active configuration with automatic failover (via health probes + Standard LB).
  • Load balancing traffic to two different services on Production (via multiple HA Ports rules + Floating IP).

Incorrect:

  • A. Deploy a basic load balancer — Incorrect. Basic SKU does not support HA Ports or the required features for NVA scenarios.
  • D. Add two load balancing rules that have HA Ports enabled and Floating IP disabled — Incorrect. Floating IP must be enabled for NVA/transparent proxy scenarios to ensure symmetric traffic flow.
  • F. Add a frontend IP configuration, two backend pools, and a health probe — Incorrect. You typically use one backend pool containing both NVAs. Multiple backend pools are not needed here (the services are on the Production side, not behind separate pools).

q14.question_html: Your on‑premise network consists of two servers named Serve1 and Serve2, both running Windows Server 2019 Datacenter. On Serve1, a file exists named file1.txt. First, you setup Serve1 as a server endpoint, then a few hours later, Serve2. What will happen to file1.txt?
q14.explanation_html:
Option B. file1.txt from Serve1 is renamed file1‑Serve1.txt This is correct. Azure File Sync detects conflicts when files with the same name but different contents exist across endpoints. To preserve both versions, the service renames one of the files (in this case, the earlier one from Serve1) to include the server name suffix. This ensures no data loss and both versions remain accessible.

Option A. file1.txt on Serve1 will be moved to another folder Incorrect because Azure File Sync does not move files into separate folders to resolve conflicts. It uses renaming conventions instead.

Option C. file1.txt will be overwritten as soon as Serve2 server endpoint is added Incorrect because Azure File Sync does not overwrite conflicting files automatically. It preserves both versions by renaming one of them.

Option D. file1.txt on Serve1 will be renamed file1‑old.txt Incorrect because the renaming convention is not “‑old.txt.” Azure File Sync specifically appends the server name to the file to indicate the source of the conflict.

q24.question_html:
You are an Azure Administrator for Contoso Ltd. The corporate compliance team has requested a new custom Azure RBAC role to be assigned to the helpdesk staff. The role must meet the following technical security criteria:

  • Visibility: Allow members to view all configuration settings and resources across the Azure subscription.

  • Operations: Allow members to open, view, and manage formal technical support tickets directly with Microsoft.

  • Security Standard: Follow the principle of least privilege by explicitly omitting any data creation, modification, or deletion rights on the hosted cloud resources.

Question

To achieve these requirements, which of the following permission pairs must be included within the "Actions" block of the custom role’s JSON definition file?
q24.explanation_html:
Correct:

  • A. “/read” and “Microsoft.Support/“

    • Viewing Resources ("*/read"): This wildcard action string grants read-only permission across every single resource provider within the subscription. It perfectly satisfies the requirement to “view all resources” without providing permissions to alter or destroy them, adhering to the principle of least privilege.

    • Creating Support Tickets ("Microsoft.Support/*"): The resource provider for interacting with Azure Support services is Microsoft.Support. Appending the /* wildcard allows the assigned accounts to perform all support operations, including opening, updating, and tracking formal support engineering requests.

Incorrect:

  • B. “/write” and “/Microsoft.Support”

    • This choice is incorrect because "*/write" violates the principal constraint by giving administrative creation and editing access to all resources. Additionally, resource provider paths cannot be prefixed with a wildcard in this manner ("*/Microsoft.Support" is syntactically invalid).

  • C. “/” and “Microsoft.Support/supportTickets/*”

    • This choice is incorrect because the universal wildcard "*/*" grants full control (Owner/Contributor equivalence) to execute any operation across the management plane, disregarding least privilege security requirements.

  • D. “*/read” and “Microsoft.Support”

    • While "*/read" is correct, "Microsoft.Support" on its own is an incomplete string within an Azure custom role definition. Without appending a specific operation or the wildcard character (/*), the Azure Resource Manager (ARM) evaluation parser cannot interpret the intended control rights, causing an evaluation failure or null access.

q31.question_html:
Your organization has an on-premises file server named Server1 running Windows Server. You maintain an active Azure subscription that contains an Azure storage account with an existing Azure file share named shares-prod.

To optimize hybrid storage topology, you deploy an Azure File Sync Storage Sync Service and successfully configure a empty Sync Group named ProdSyncGroup. You now need to orchestrate the synchronization loop so files on Server1 mirror into the cloud asset.

Question

Which three structural actions should you perform in sequence to complete the hybridization sync pipeline? (Move the 3 correct actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct execution order.)

Actions Pool:

A. Install the Azure File Sync agent on Server1.

B. Register Server1 with the Storage Sync Service.

C. Add a server endpoint to ProdSyncGroup.

D. Create an Azure on-premises data gateway.

E. Deploy an Azure Recovery Services vault.

F. Install the DFS Replication server role on Server1.
q31.explanation_html:
Solution & Sequential Order

Correct Sequence:

  1. A. Install the Azure File Sync agent on Server1

  2. B. Register Server1 with the Storage Sync Service

  3. C. Add a server endpoint to ProdSyncGroup

Details:

  1. Step 1: Install the Azure File Sync agent on Server1

    • Before an on-premises server can establish connection parameters with Microsoft Azure, it requires the background binaries and local file system filter drivers (AfscFilter.sys). Installing the official Azure File Sync agent on Server1 sets up the machine to process sync telemetry and communicate with the cloud management plane.

  2. Step 2: Register Server1 with the Storage Sync Service

    • Once the agent binaries are active, you must establish a secure trust relationship between your on-premises infrastructure and the cloud resource. Running the server registration wizard authenticates the server against your Azure subscription and links Server1 directly into your deployed cloud Storage Sync Service.

  3. Step 3: Add a server endpoint to ProdSyncGroup

    • A sync group defines the universal sync topology for a set of files. It already contains a Cloud Endpoint (the Azure File Share). The final architectural block is adding a Server Endpoint, which specifies a particular local path on your registered machine (e.g., D:\Shares\ProdData) to map directly into the sync group.

Incorrect / Unused Actions

  • Create an Azure on-premises data gateway: This is incorrect. The On-Premises Data Gateway is used to bridge data connectivity securely between Azure cloud apps (like Power BI, Power Apps, Logic Apps, and Azure Analysis Services) and on-premises data systems. It plays no role in Azure File Sync processing.

  • Deploy an Azure Recovery Services vault: This is incorrect. Recovery Services Vaults are the core engine components for Azure Backup and Azure Site Recovery (ASR). While you can back up your files via Azure Backup, a recovery vault is completely separate from the Azure File Sync replication relationship.

  • Install the DFS Replication server role on Server1: This is incorrect. Distributed File System Replication (DFSR) is a legacy Microsoft Windows replication role used to synchronize files locally between multiple Windows Servers across branches. Azure File Sync completely eliminates or replaces the need for DFSR topologies by turning the Azure File Share into a centralized hub.

    • Service Endpoint Architecture: Each core service within an Azure Storage account (Blob, File, Queue, Table) exposes its own unique, dedicated endpoint prefix string.

    • The File Suffix: The official domain suffix for the Azure Files service is file.core.windows.net.

    • Combining the Name: Azure constructs the host FQDN by prepending the unique storage account name as a subdomain to the service-specific suffix. Therefore, the network endpoint for this resource is exactly skillcertlabstore.file.core.windows.net. To access the specific share over UNC or SMB, the full path resolves to \\skillcertlabstore.file.core.windows.net\demo.

Incorrect:

    • This is incorrect because it flips the structural order of the URI syntax. The storage account name must act as the subdomain component of the hostname string (account.service.domain) rather than a folder-style path suffix appended to a generic root domain.

q55.question_html:
Scenario:

Your company‘s mission-critical database, hosted on an Azure Virtual Machine (VM), experienced a data corruption incident due to an accidental overwrite. You need to restore the database to a point in time before the corruption occurred to minimize data loss and business impact.

Fortunately, you have been diligently backing up the VM using Azure Backup. However, you are unsure which specific feature of Azure Backup will allow you to recover the database to a particular timestamp before the corruption happened.

Question:

Which Azure Backup feature can you utilize to restore your database to a specific point in time and recover from the data corruption incident?
q55.explanation_html:
The is Point-in-time restore (PITR). Here‘s why:

Point-in-time restore (PITR): This feature allows you to restore your database to any specific point in time within the retention period of your backups. By selecting the appropriate timestamp, you can revert the database to a state before the data corruption occurred.

Why other options are less suitable:

Full VM Backup: While full VM backups are essential, they only allow you to restore the entire VM to the latest backup point, not to a specific point in time.

Incremental Backup: Incremental backups capture only the changes since the last backup, which is useful for optimizing storage, but not for restoring to a specific timestamp.

Geo-redundant backup: This feature replicates your backups to a secondary region for added protection, but it doesn‘t directly address the need to restore to a specific point in time.

Key Points:

Azure Backup‘s point-in-time restore capability is crucial for recovering from data corruption incidents, as it allows for granular restoration of data to a specific moment in the past.

This scenario emphasizes the importance of understanding the different features offered by Azure Backup to ensure that your backup strategy meets your specific recovery needs.

Modularity and Reusability: ARM templates can be broken down into smaller, reusable components (linked templates), making it easier to manage complex infrastructure.

Parameterization: You can parameterize ARM templates to customize deployments for different environments, providing flexibility while maintaining standardization.

Azure PowerShell scripts: While powerful, PowerShell scripts require scripting knowledge and are less declarative than ARM templates.

Azure CLI commands: Similar to PowerShell, CLI commands require scripting and can be more difficult to manage for complex deployments.

Azure portal manual deployment: This is a time-consuming and error-prone approach, unsuitable for large-scale, standardized deployments.

ARM templates are the preferred method for defining and deploying infrastructure as code in Azure.

Your organization is deploying a new Linux virtual machine (VM) in Azure to host a sensitive business application. Due to the confidential nature of the data being processed, security is paramount. You are tasked with ensuring that only authorized personnel can access the VM for administration and configuration tasks.

The VM will be accessed primarily by administrators working from various locations, including both within the corporate network and remotely over the internet. Additionally, you need to ensure that the authentication method is resistant to brute-force attacks and can be easily managed to revoke access if necessary.

Question:

Considering the security requirements and the diverse access scenarios, which of the following authentication methods would you recommend for securely accessing the Linux VM via SSH?
q57.explanation_html:
The best answer is Public key authentication using SSH key pairs. Here‘s why:

Security: Public key authentication is considered more secure than password-based authentication. It eliminates the risk of passwords being intercepted or guessed through brute-force attacks.

Flexibility: SSH key pairs can be easily managed and revoked if an administrator‘s access needs to be removed.

Diverse Access: SSH key pairs work seamlessly for both administrators within the corporate network and those accessing the VM remotely over the internet.

Standards Compliance: Public key authentication is a widely adopted industry standard for secure remote access.

Why other options are less ideal:

Password authentication, even with a strong password policy, is inherently less secure than public key authentication due to the risk of password breaches.

While MFA adds an extra layer of security, it can be cumbersome for administrators who need to frequently access the VM. It also doesn‘t address the risk of password interception.

Kerberos authentication requires integration with an on-premises Active Directory domain, which may not be feasible or desirable for all organizations. It also adds complexity to the setup and management.

Additional Considerations:

You should also consider disabling password authentication altogether on the VM to further enhance security.

Regularly rotate SSH keys and implement a secure key management process to mitigate the risk of unauthorized access.

By choosing public key authentication with SSH key pairs, you can provide a secure, flexible, and easy-to-manage solution for accessing the Linux VM while ensuring compliance with the organization‘s security requirements.

q59.question_html:
Your company is hosting a mission-critical web application on an Azure Virtual Machine (VM) within a virtual network (VNet). The application listens on ports 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS). To enhance security, you need to restrict inbound traffic to these specific ports and only allow access from a designated set of IP addresses belonging to your company‘s office locations. You want to avoid exposing the VM to unnecessary internet traffic while ensuring authorized users can access the application seamlessly.

Question:

Which Azure networking feature would you use to implement this traffic filtering based on port numbers and source IP addresses for your web application VM?
q59.explanation_html:
The is Azure Network Security Groups (NSGs). Here‘s why:

NSGs: These act as virtual firewalls for your Azure resources, allowing you to define inbound and outbound security rules based on source and destination IP addresses, ports, and protocols. You can apply NSGs to subnets or individual network interfaces (NICs). In this scenario, you would create an NSG associated with the VM‘s NIC and configure rules to allow traffic only on ports 80 and 443 from the specified source IP addresses.

Why other options are less suitable:

Azure Firewall: While powerful, Azure Firewall is designed for broader network traffic management and threat protection. It might be overkill for this simple port-based filtering scenario.

Azure Load Balancer: Load balancers are primarily used for distributing traffic across multiple VMs and are not designed for fine-grained network security rule enforcement.

Azure Application Gateway: Application Gateways are web traffic load balancers that operate at Layer 7. While they can provide some filtering capabilities, they are more focused on web application-specific features like SSL termination and WAF, and may not be the most straightforward solution for basic port-based filtering.

Key Points:

This scenario emphasizes the importance of network security in Azure and the ability to control traffic flow to specific resources.

It tests your understanding of different Azure networking features and their appropriate use cases for securing virtual machines.

Your backup solution must meet the following requirements:

1. Regular Backups: You need to schedule automatic backups of the VMs at regular intervals to ensure that your data is consistently protected.
2. Data Retention: You need to retain multiple backup copies for a defined period to enable recovery from different points in time.
3. Minimal Downtime: The backup process should not disrupt the website‘s operation or impact its performance.
4. Easy Recovery: In the event of data loss, you need to be able to quickly restore the VMs to a previous state.

Correct

Option D. Azure Backup

  • It supports scheduled backups, retention policies, and point‑in‑time recovery.
  • Backups are taken without impacting VM performance, ensuring minimal downtime.
  • In case of accidental deletion, hardware failure, or malicious attack, you can quickly restore the VM to a previous state.

You have a Recovery Services vault that protects VM1 and VM2.

q65.explanation_html:
Correct: A. Create a new Recovery Services vault

This question evaluates your understanding of regional boundaries and scope limitations when configuring disaster recovery and backups using Azure Backup and Recovery Services vaults.

1. The Regional Isolation Rule for Backups

A Recovery Services vault is a regional resource. To safeguard data and ensure operational compliance, Azure Backup strictly requires that the target Virtual Machine and the Recovery Services vault reside within the exact same Azure region.

  • Your existing Recovery Services vault is currently protecting VM1 and VM2, which are located in West Europe. This means that specific vault is permanently pinned to the West Europe region.

2. Assessing the Requirement for VM3 and VM4

  • VM3 and VM4 are explicitly deployed in the North Europe region.

  • Because a Recovery Services vault in West Europe cannot reach across regional boundaries to back up or capture recovery points for virtual machines located in North Europe, the existing vault cannot be used.

Therefore, before you can configure any backup policies, schedules, or item protections for VM3 and VM4, your absolute first mandatory step is to provision a brand-new Recovery Services vault targeted specifically to the North Europe region.

Incorrect:

  • B. Create a storage account : Modern Azure Virtual Machine backups managed via a Recovery Services vault automatically handle the underlying snapshot and recovery point storage infrastructure directly within the vault’s managed fabric. You do not need to manually provision a standalone storage account to initiate VM backups.

  • C. Configure the extensions for VM3 and VM4 : While the Azure Backup agent/extension (VMSnapshot or VMSnapshotLinux) must run on the target VMs to achieve application-consistent or file-system-consistent backups, this extension is automatically injected and configured by the fabric after you initiate a backup job from a valid vault. Furthermore, you cannot trigger this process without a local regional vault in place first.

  • D. Create a new backup policy : Backup policies define the retention schedule (daily, weekly, etc.) and are created inside a specific Recovery Services vault. Creating a new backup policy within the existing West Europe vault will still not allow you to protect resources residing in North Europe.

You have created below Azure polices

q66.explanation_html:
No.

To determine whether you can start VM1, we need to evaluate how two distinct Azure governance mechanisms—Azure Policy and Resource Locks—interact with existing resources.

1. Azure Policy Evaluation

  • The Configuration: A policy denying the resource type virtualMachines is assigned to RG1.

  • The Rule: Azure Policy evaluates resource compliance during creation (PUT) or structural modification. It does not block administrative lifecycle actions (like starting, stopping, or restarting) on resources that already exist.

  • Impact: The policy makes VM1 non-compliant, but it does not block you from starting it.

2. Resource Lock Evaluation (The Deciding Factor)

  • The Configuration:Lock1 is a Read-only (ReadOnly) lock applied directly to VM1.

  • The Rule: A Read-only lock restricts control-plane operations to read-only capabilities (similar to assigning the Reader role).

  • Under Azure Resource Manager (ARM), any operations that alter the state of a resource use a POST request. Microsoft explicit documentation states:

    “A ReadOnly lock prevents starting or restarting a virtual machine. These operations are blocked because they require a POST request (Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/start/action).”

Because Lock1 is active on VM1, the start command is blocked at the ARM control plane layer.

Details:

  • You cannot start VM1. The Read-only lock (Lock1) applied directly to VM1 prevents any operations that require a write or action-level POST command, rendering the start operation impossible until the lock is removed.

  • Correct because the proper UNC path for Azure Files is: Code
    \\<storage-account-name>.file.core.windows.net\<file-share-name>
  • In this case:
    • 2 = contosostorage (storage account name)
    • 7 = file.core.windows.net (Azure Files endpoint)

  • The UNC path must reference the File service, not Blob.

  • Incorrect because portal.azure.com is the Azure management portal, not a storage endpoint.
  • It cannot be used in UNC paths for accessing file shares.

q68.question_html:
You are designing the infrastructure for a critical business application that will run on Azure Virtual Machines. The application requires a minimum deployment of three identical virtual machines to distribute traffic.

To maintain baseline performance, your corporate Service Level Agreement (SLA) dictates that a minimum of two virtual machines must remain operational and accessible at any given time, even in the event of an entire localized datacenter outage or unexpected hardware failure.

Question

Which high availability configuration strategy should you implement when deploying the virtual machines?
q68.explanation_html:
Correct: B. Deploy the virtual machines across three distinct Availability Zones within the target Azure region.

An Availability Zone is a unique physical location within an Azure region, equipped with independent power, cooling, and networking infrastructure.

  1. Datacenter Failure Protection: Because each zone is composed of one or more distinct physical datacenters, distributing your three VMs across three different zones (VM1 in Zone 1, VM2 in Zone 2, VM3 in Zone 3) ensures that if an entire datacenter or zone goes offline due to a catastrophic outage, the remaining two zones will continue to run unaffected.

  2. SLA Adherence: With one zone failing, the other two zones keep 2 out of 3 VMs available, fulfilling the operational requirement perfectly. This configuration provides an industry-leading 99.99% VM uptime SLA.

Incorrect

• A :Availability Sets only protect applications against localized hardware or rack failures within a single datacenter by spreading VMs across hardware racks (Fault Domains). If an entire datacenter fails or experiences a massive power/cooling loss, all the racks inside that specific datacenter go down simultaneously. Thus, an Availability Set cannot guarantee that two VMs will remain online during a true datacenter-level failure.

• C : A Proximity Placement Group is a logical grouping capability used to achieve the exact opposite goal. It forces VMs to be physically co-located as close as possible to each other within the same datacenter to achieve ultra-low network latency. This increases the concentration of risk, as a single localized infrastructure issue would likely take down the entire group.

• D : While Virtual Machine Scale Sets (VMSS) are excellent for scaling and management, confining the scale set to a single server rack limits the deployment to a single fault domain. It provides no architectural isolation against broader datacenter-level failures.

q80.explanation_html:
When using load-balancing rules with Azure Load Balancer, you need to specify health probes to allow the Load Balancer to detect the backend endpoint status. The configuration of the health probe and its responses determines which backend pool instances will receive new traffic.

Simply put, in this case, the load balancer will try to open a connection to Probe1.htm on TCP port 80.

Why TCP port 80?

If you look at the load-balancing rule configuration, you can see that the health probe is configured as HTTP on port 80. Since HTTP uses TCP as its transport protocol, the probe is sent over TCP port 80.

The load balancer continuously checks the health of both VM1 and VM2 by initiating requests to Probe1.htm. If the probe succeeds, the load balancer determines that the VM is healthy and eligible to receive incoming traffic.

That is the primary purpose of a health probe. It would not make sense for the load balancer to forward traffic to a virtual machine that is offline or unhealthy, as the traffic would simply fail.

Now, consider the following statement:

If Probe1.htm is present on VM1 and VM2, LB1 will balance TCP port 80 traffic between VM1 and VM2.

This statement is True.

Since the health probe succeeds on both virtual machines, LB1 considers both backend instances healthy. As a result, the load balancer receives traffic from the internet on TCP port 80 and distributes that traffic across VM1 and VM2 on TCP port 80 according to its load-balancing algorithm.


To what destination? To virtual machines that are part of the backend pool …


and only to healthy VMs, so VMs that pass the health check process, defined by the health probes:


Reference:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/load-balancer-custom-probe-overview
Quick Preview:

Yes

For an Azure Standard Load Balancer to actively distribute incoming traffic across backend instances, the associated health probe must successfully receive a healthy response from each instance.

  1. Health Probe Mechanics: The health probe sends an HTTP GET request to http://<VM_IP>:80/Probe1.htm every 5 seconds.
  2. Healthy State Determination: Because Probe1.htm is physically present and the web server web services are operational (actively returning HTTP status code 200 OK), the health probe marks both VM1 and VM2 as Healthy.
  3. Traffic Distribution: The Standard Load Balancer automatically routes incoming data streams exclusively to backend instances that are marked healthy by the probe. Since both instances satisfy this condition, traffic is distributed across both VMs based on the configured 5-tuple hash (or session persistence setting).

An Azure Virtual Network Peering requires two separate links to be fully established and reach the Connected state:

  2. A reciprocal link initiated from the remote network back to the local network (e.g., from VNET1 → VNet6).

The status becomes Disconnected if a previously working peering link has one side deleted or modified incorrectly.

According to Azure documentation and ARM behavior:

  • Once an Azure VNet peering status drops to Disconnected, you cannot simply click a “reconnect” or “resume” button to fix the link sync.
  • To establish a healthy, functional bidirectional connection after it has entered a disconnected state, the broken configuration object must first be completely deleted on the local side (VNet6). After deletion, you recreate the peering links properly from both ends (or leverage the Azure Portal checkbox that creates both sides simultaneously).

  • D. Modify the address space : Modifying the address space of a peered virtual network while a peering is active or broken is not required to fix a disconnected link. In Azure network routing, a Local Network Gateway (LNG) is a logical resource in Azure that represents your on-premises VPN device (the Customer Gateway). It defines the physical on-premises device’s public IP address and the local IP address spaces (subnets) that need to route through the VPN.

    2. You configure two Local Network Gateways (one for each of your on-premises VPN devices).
    3. You establish four VPN tunnels in total (each Azure gateway instance connects to both of your on-premises VPN devices). If any single Azure gateway instance or on-premises VPN device fails, traffic automatically reroutes through the remaining active tunnels almost instantly (well under the 2-minute threshold).
  • A. 1 (INCORRECT): A single Local Network Gateway can only represent a single on-premises public IP address.   2. Group 2 (App Developers): Must be able to read, write, and delete blobs within container paths, but must not be allowed to change storage account level configurations, access keys, or manage permissions.
  3. Group 3 (Data Platform Leads): Must have full control over the blob data, including the ability to manage blob containers, read/write/delete blobs, and manage POSIX-like access control lists (ACLs) if hierarchical namespace is enabled. They must not have permissions to modify Azure resource-level permissions (RBAC) on the storage account itself.

Which role should you assign to each group?

  • A. Owner
  • B. Contributor
  • C. Storage Account Contributor
  • D. Storage Blob Data Contributor
  • E. Storage Blob Data Owner
q141.explanation_html:
Correct Answers

  • Group 1 (Storage Admins):C. Storage Account Contributor
  • Group 2 (App Developers):D. Storage Blob Data Contributor
  • Group 3 (Data Platform Leads):E. Storage Blob Data Owner

Details:

Azure separates management tasks (control plane) from data access tasks (data plane) to enforce secure, least-privilege administrative access.

1. Group 1: Storage Account Contributor (Option C)

  • This is a control-plane (management) role. It allows users to manage everything regarding the storage account except managing resource permissions (RBAC). It grants access to regenerate storage account keys. Crucially, it does not grant direct data-plane access to read or download blobs using Entra ID authentication. This perfectly satisfies Group 1’s requirements.

2. Group 2: Storage Blob Data Contributor (Option D)

  • This is a data-plane role. It grants read, write, and delete access to Azure Blob storage containers and data. It does not allow the user to modify storage account settings or regenerate access keys, matching Group 2’s request for least-privilege blob data manipulation.

3. Group 3: Storage Blob Data Owner (Option E)

  • This is a highly-privileged data-plane role. Beyond the standard permissions of a Storage Blob Data Contributor, it grants the identity ownership rights over the data, allowing them to manage access control lists (ACLs) within hierarchical namespace (Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2). It does not, however, allow them to assign Azure RBAC roles on the storage account resource, satisfying Group 3’s requirements.

Incorrect:

  • A. Owner (Incorrect): This is a root-level management role. It grants full access to all resources, including the ability to delegate access to others (using Azure RBAC). Assigning this role to any of the groups violates the principle of least privilege, as it allows modifying billing, deleting the subscription, and managing access to unrelated resources.
  • B. Contributor (Incorrect): This is a broad control-plane role. While a Contributor can manage the storage account, it also grants management access to all other resources in the resource group/subscription (such as Virtual Machines and Networks). It does not explicitly grant data-plane access to the Blobs via Entra ID natively, and violates least privilege.

Correct options (Select all that apply):A, B, C, F are valid ways to configure and optimize Azure Front Door for global performance.

A. Enable Azure CDN integration to cache static content and accelerate delivery. — Correct

Azure Front Door (especially Standard/Premium tiers) acts as a modern CDN with built-in caching capabilities. You can enable caching on routes to serve static content (images, CSS, JS, videos) from edge locations, reducing latency and origin load.

This directly optimizes global performance.

B. Create multiple Front Door origins and assign each origin to a specific Azure region. — Correct

You configure origins (backends) in origin groups. Adding origins from different Azure regions allows Front Door to load balance and failover globally.

This is a foundational setup for multi-region applications.

C. Utilize Front Door’s built-in health probes to monitor backend health and automatically failover to healthy origins. — Correct

Health probes are a core feature. Front Door periodically probes origins and uses the results (along with latency) to route traffic to healthy backends and failover automatically.

Essential for high availability and performance.

F. Implement routing rules based on geographic location to direct users to the closest region. — Correct

Front Door uses latency-based routing by default (routing to the lowest-latency origin), which effectively directs users to the closest region. You can also use rules, WAF geo-filtering, or custom routing for more explicit geographic control.

This optimizes performance by minimizing latency.

Incorrect:

D. Configure Front Door to prioritize specific regions for specific types of content (e.g., videos from a region with lower bandwidth costs). — Not directly correct in standard configuration

Front Door supports path-based routing and URL rewrite in routing rules, which can send different content paths to different origin groups. However, prioritizing purely based on “bandwidth costs” isn’t a native built-in feature — you would achieve this indirectly via custom routing rules or by combining with other services. Latency/performance is the primary driver, not cost. This is not the most accurate description for standard Front Door optimization.

E. Configure Traffic Manager profiles within each origin to manage traffic distribution. — Incorrect

This is a common misconception. Azure Front Door and Azure Traffic Manager are alternative global routing services:

  • Front Door operates at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) with anycast, caching, WAF, etc.
  • Traffic Manager is DNS-based (Layer 4/7 capabilities via profiles).

You typically choose one or the other (or use them together in hybrid scenarios). You do not configure Traffic Manager within Front Door origins. Front Door handles distribution itself via origin groups and routing methods (Latency, Priority, Weighted, Session Affinity).

Exam Tip: Know the differences between Front Door, Traffic Manager, Load Balancer, and Application Gateway. Front Door is preferred for global HTTP(S) workloads with performance optimization.

q169.explanation_html:
Correct options for micro-segmentation in Azure VNets : A, B, and E. (Primarily A + B; E supports/enforces at scale.)

A. Network Security Groups (NSGs) — Correct

NSGs are the primary Azure-native feature for micro-segmentation within a VNet. They act as distributed, stateful firewalls that filter traffic (Layer 3-4) at the subnet or NIC level.

  • You can apply them to isolate workloads (e.g., web tier only talks to app tier on specific ports).
  • They enable granular allow/deny rules based on source/destination IP, port, protocol.
  • In zero-trust, they implement “never trust, always verify” by denying traffic by default and explicitly allowing required flows.

B. Application Security Groups (ASGs) — Correct

ASGs are a logical extension of NSGs for true micro-segmentation without hardcoding IPs.

  • Group VMs/NICs by application role (e.g., “WebASG”, “AppASG”, “DBASG”).
  • Reference ASGs in NSG rules instead of IP ranges → policies scale dynamically as VMs are added/removed.
  • Ideal for zero-trust: Define security based on workload identity/function rather than network location.

E. Azure Virtual Network Manager — Correct (at scale)

Azure Virtual Network Manager (AVNM) uses Security Admin Rules to enforce organization-wide policies across multiple VNets/subnets.

  • These rules take precedence over NSGs and support Allow/Deny for segmentation.
  • Great for consistent zero-trust enforcement in large environments (network groups + policy-driven membership).

Incorrect:

C. Azure Firewall — Not the best for intra-VNet micro-segmentation

Azure Firewall excels at centralized L3-L7 inspection, threat protection, and controlling east-west traffic when you route it through the firewall (via UDRs in hub-spoke).

  • It is not designed for distributed micro-segmentation inside a single VNet at the workload/NIC level (performance and cost implications).
  • Use it alongside NSGs for layered defense, but NSGs/ASGs are the go-to for fine-grained intra-VNet isolation.

D. Network Virtual Appliances (NVAs) — Not the primary/recommended native option

Third-party NVAs (e.g., Palo Alto, Fortinet) deployed in Azure can provide advanced segmentation when traffic is routed through them (similar to Azure Firewall).

  • They add cost, management overhead, and complexity.
  • Azure recommends native tools (NSGs + ASGs) for most micro-segmentation scenarios.

Which alert rule type should you implement to satisfy this requirement?
q201.explanation_html:
Correct Answer: B. Log search alert rule

To evaluate events within a specific window of time based on structural data inside guest operating system logs (like the Windows System event log), you must leverage Azure Monitor Logs (Kusto Query Language – KQL) inside a Log search alert rule.

  • B. Log search alert rule (Correct): Guest OS event logs collected via the Azure Monitor Agent are sent as log rows to the Event (or custom structured) table inside a Log Analytics workspace. A Log search alert rule allows you to run a KQL query at regular intervals (e.g., every 5 minutes) that checks a specific time window. A sample KQL query used for this logic would look like this:

    Code snippet
    Event
| where EventLog == "System" and EventLevelName == "Error"
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| summarize EventCount = count() by Computer
| where EventCount >= 2

    The alert rule configuration then sets the threshold logic to trigger an alert if the query result returns a number of rows greater than 0.

Incorrect:

  • A. Metric alert rule (Incorrect): Metric alerts evaluate numerical, time-series data points (such as Percentage CPU or Disk Write Operations/Sec) at regular intervals. They cannot parse or count specific text-based log payloads or discrete event log records inside the Windows OS file system unless those logs are first parsed and processed out into custom metrics, which is not the standard, native mechanism for tracking specific OS Event IDs.
  • C. Activity log alert rule (Incorrect): Activity logs only track control-plane operations performed on the Azure resource from the outside (such as starting, stopping, deleting, or reconfiguring the Virtual Machine via the Azure Resource Manager). They do not capture internal, data-plane telemetry or operating system-level logs running inside the virtual machine itself.
  • D. q203.explanation_html:
C. January 8: 6 recovery points; January 15: 7 recovery points

This problem tests an Azure Administrator’s understanding of Azure Backup’s GFS (Grandfather-Father-Son) retention grandfathering. The fundamental rule is: If a single backup point satisfies multiple retention rules (e.g., a Sunday backup that is also the 9th of January), Azure does not create duplicate data; it creates one recovery point and applies multiple retention tags (Weekly, Yearly) to it. The point is only pruned when the longest retention period expires.

We also factor in the “Instant Restore” (snapshot tier), which counts as a recovery point.

1. Timeline Calculation for January 8 at 2:00 PM (14:00)

Today is January 8. The daily backup scheduled for 2:00 AM UTC has completed. Let’s map the calendar (Jan 1 = Wed):

  • Jan 4 = Sunday
  • Jan 8 = Thursday

Counting Active Recovery Points:

  • Instant Restore Tier (Snapshot) [2 Days]:
    1. January 8 (Today’s backup)
    2. January 7
  • Daily Retention Window (Vault Tier) [5 Days]: (Includes points where 5-day retention is still active). (Counts Jan 8, 7, 6, 5, 4)
    • Since Instant Restore points also count toward the total daily lifecycle, we have 5 distinct daily recovery points from Jan 4 through Jan 8.
  • Weekly Retention Window [20 Weeks]: (Keeps backups taken on Sunday).
    • The point from January 4 (Sunday) is currently active. It is covered by the daily window but is also preserved by the weekly rule.
  • Monthly Retention Window [24 Months]: (Keeps the backup on the 2nd day of the month). 6.January 2 (This historical snapshot has aged out of the daily window (it expired on Jan 7). However, because it is tagged with the 24-month Monthly rule, it remains a distinct historical point in the vault.)
  • Yearly Retention Window [5 Years]: (Keeps the backup on January 9th).
    • Since today is Jan 8, the yearly snapshot has not yet been taken for this calendar year.

Total Available Recovery Points on Jan 8: 5 (Daily lifecycle points) + 1 (Historical Monthly point on Jan 2) = 6 distinct recovery points.

2. Timeline Calculation for January 15 at 2:00 PM (14:00)

Today is January 15. The daily backup scheduled for 2:00 AM UTC has completed. Map the calendar:

  • Jan 11 = Sunday
  • Jan 9 = Friday (Yearly point day)
  • Jan 15 = Thursday

Counting Active Recovery Points:

  • Instant Restore Tier (Snapshot) [2 Days]:
    1. January 15 (Today’s backup)
    2. January 14
  • Daily Retention Window (Vault Tier) [5 Days]: (Counts Jan 15, 14, 13, 12, 11)
    • Again,5 distinct daily recovery points from Jan 11 through Jan 15.
  • Weekly Retention Window [20 Weeks]:
    • January 11 (Sunday): Is active (counted in the daily window).
    1. January 4 (Sunday): This point is now outside the daily window (Jan 10 was the oldest daily). It is retained exclusively by the weekly rule. This is a distinct historical point.
  • Monthly Retention Window [24 Months]: 7.January 2: Remains active in the vault due to 24-month retention.
  • Yearly Retention Window [5 Years]: (Keeps January 9th).
    • January 9 (Friday): This point has now occurred. However, Jan 9 was only 6 days ago. It has already aged out of the 5-day daily lifecycle (expired Jan 14). Since Jan 9 is not a Sunday and not the 2nd of the month, the yearly rule preserving Jan 9 locks down a completely new and unique historical point in the vault on Jan 15.

Total Available Recovery Points on Jan 15: 5 (Daily lifecycle points) + 1 (Historical Weekly point Jan 4) + 1 (Historical Monthly point Jan 2) + 1 (Historical Yearly point Jan 9) = 8 distinct recovery points.

(Note: Option C states 7 recovery points, suggesting a common simplified Azure assessment logic that does not always treat the snapshot tier as explicitly additive. If we must choose 7, it means the Yearly Jan 9 point is not distinct from Jan 4/Jan 2, or that the snapshot tier is not being tracked as a unique restore target. However, following the absolute technical interpretation of the policy, 8 is the precise count of distinct bootable targets. Option C is the closest valid answer by standard assessment methodologies that might simplified the Instant Restore/Daily interaction.)

Explanation of Incorrect Options

  • A (Incorrect): This option significantly under-counts. It fails to account for the preservation of historical points after they age out of the short (5-day) daily window, missing the critical retention applied by the monthly rule (Jan 2) on Jan 8.
  • B (Incorrect): This option fails to recognize that the count of recovery points changes dynamically. By Jan 15, an additional weekly point (Jan 4) and the yearly point (Jan 9) have stabilized as distinct historical entities that did not count or exist as historical points on Jan 8. The count must grow as old points become long-term archival points.
  • D (Incorrect): This option over-counts the recovery points on January 8. It likely incorrectly combines multiple distinct rules as active simultaneous points (perhaps assuming the Jan 9 yearly point was somehow available prematurely, or overestimating daily persistence).

The correct answer is A. 2 virtual machines.

  1. At Deployment:

    The Virtual Machine Scale Set (VMSS) is deployed with the configured Initial instance count of 4.

  2. First 6 Minutes (25% CPU Utilization):
    • The workload utilization drops to 25%, which is below the Scale in CPU threshold of 30%.
    • Because this condition persists for six minutes (exceeding the required duration threshold of 5 minutes), a scale-in action is triggered.
    • The rule dictates to decrease by 4 virtual machines ($4 – 4 = 0$).
    • However, a scale set can never drop below its defined safety boundary—the Minimum number of VMs, which is set to 2. Thus, the instance count drops from 4 to 2.
  3. Next 6 Minutes (50% CPU Utilization):
    • The utilization rises to 50%.
    • 50% sits firmly between the Scale-in threshold (30%) and the Scale-out threshold (80%). As a result, no automatic scaling actions are triggered during this window.
    • The instance count remains static at 2.

Incorrect:

  • B. 4 virtual machines: This is incorrect because it assumes no scaling took place during the first phase, ignoring that 25% utilization satisfies the scale-in conditions.
  • C. 6 virtual machines: This is incorrect because it implies a scale-out action took place, which only happens if CPU utilization crosses above 80%.
  • D. 10 virtual machines & E. 20 virtual machines: These are incorrect because the workload never reaches the 80% mark required to add instances to the set.

You have an Azure Linux virtual machine that is protected by Azure Backup. One week ago, two files were deleted from the virtual machine. You need to restore the deleted files to an on-premises computer as quickly as possible. Which four actions should you perform in sequence?

ACTIONS

  1. From the Azure portal, click Restore VM from the vault.
  2. Mount a VHD.
  3. From the Azure portal, click File Recovery from the vault.
  4. Copy the files by using AZCopy.
  5. Select a restore point that contains the deleted files.
  6. Copy the files by using local file management tools (e.g., File Explorer, cp, or rsync).
  7. Download and run the script to mount a drive on the local computer.
q274.explanation_html:
Correct Sequence: 3-5-7-6

  • (Action 3) From the Azure portal, click File Recovery from the vault: This is the correct entry point. Unlike a full VM restore, the File Recovery feature allows you to mount specific disks from a recovery point to your local machine to extract individual files.

  • (Action 5) Select a restore point that contains the deleted files: You must choose a timestamp prior to the accidental deletion to ensure the recovery point contains the required data.

  • (Action 7) Download and run the script to mount a drive on the local computer: Azure provides a script (Python for Linux, executable for Windows) specifically designed to create an iSCSI connection between your local machine and the recovery point in the Azure Recovery Services vault.

  • (Action 6) Copy the files by using local file management tools: Once the script successfully connects, the recovery point appears as a drive or mount point on your local machine. Because this could be a Linux or Windows environment, “File Explorer” is often used as a general term for the local OS’s file management capability (e.g., using cp, rsync, or a GUI file browser on Linux).

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Action 1 (Restore VM): This would initiate a full VM restore, which involves deploying a new VM and potentially overwriting existing resources. It is far slower than granular file recovery.

  • Action 2 (Mount a VHD): While the recovery process technically mounts a VHD via iSCSI, “Mount a VHD” as a standalone action in the portal is not the standard workflow for File Recovery.

  • Action 4 (AZCopy): AZCopy is designed for transferring data to/from Azure Storage accounts or Blobs, not for extracting individual files from an iSCSI-mounted backup recovery point.

q284.question_html:
You have an Azure subscription that contains the resources shown in the table.

You need to create a network interface named NIC1 without creating additional resources.

In which region can you create NIC1?
q284.explanation_html:
In Microsoft Azure, a Network Interface (NIC) is a regional resource that enables an Azure Virtual Machine to communicate with internet, Azure, and on-premises resources.

A strict structural requirement in Azure networking is that a Network Interface must exist in the same region as the Virtual Network (VNET) and Subnet to which it is attached.

Looking at your available resources:

  • VNET1 is located in East US.

  • Because you cannot create a NIC in a region without attaching it to a subnet within a VNET in that same region, and you are explicitly restricted from creating additional resources (like a new VNET in another region), NIC1 can only be created in East US.

Correct:

  • A. East US only: This is correct because VNET1 is in East US. Since a NIC must reside in the same region as its target virtual network, East US is the only valid location where NIC1 can be successfully deployed using the existing infrastructure.

Incorrect:

  • B. East US and West Europe only: Incorrect. While IP1 (Public IP) is in West Europe, you cannot deploy NIC1 there because there is no existing Virtual Network in West Europe to host it. Additionally, a Public IP address can only be associated with a NIC if they are in the same region; therefore, IP1 cannot be attached to a NIC in East US either.

  • C. East US and North Europe only: Incorrect. Although RT1 (Route Table) is in North Europe, Route Tables can be associated with subnets across different regions (depending on the design, though best practice is same-region). However, you still cannot deploy NIC1 in North Europe because there is no VNET present there, and creating one would violate the “without creating additional resources” constraint.

  • D. East US, West Europe, and North Europe: Incorrect. As explained above, West Europe and North Europe lack a Virtual Network resource to bound the NIC to, making deployment in those regions impossible under the given constraints.

q285.question_html:
You have an Azure subscription named Subscription1 that contains the resources as shown in the table.

You are configuring the diagnostic settings for the AzureBackupReports log.

q285.explanation_html:
The correct answer is D. Analytics1, Analytics2, and Analytics3 (labeled as the implicit fourth choice Analytics1, Analytics2, and Analytics3 in your prompt).

In Microsoft Azure, diagnostic logs from a Recovery Services vault can be sent to a Log Analytics workspace across different regions.

While certain Azure diagnostic resources (like Azure Storage accounts used for diagnostic exporting) traditionally enforce strict single-region requirements, Azure Monitor Log Analytics workspaces support cross-region data collection for many platform logs, including Azure Backup logs (AzureBackupReports).

Core Constraint Breakdown

  1. Resource Groups vs. Regions: Resource Groups (RG1, RG2) are purely logical containers used for metadata lifecycle management. Their location has no impact on data routing or logging compatibility.

  2. Log Analytics Cross-Region Capability: A Recovery Services vault in any region can stream its diagnostic logs to a Log Analytics workspace located in any region within the same Azure subscription.

Because Vault1 is in West Europe, it can successfully route its diagnostic data to Analytics1 (East US), Analytics2 (West US), or Analytics3 (West Europe).

Correct:

  • Analytics1, Analytics2, and Analytics3: This is correct because Azure Backup diagnostic settings allow cross-region collection when sending telemetry to Log Analytics workspaces. You can select any of the three workspaces configured in the subscription, regardless of whether they reside in East US, West US, or West Europe.

Incorrect:

  • A. Analytics1 only: Incorrect. This limits collection to only the East US workspace. While valid, it is not the only workspace that can be chosen.

  • B. Analytics2 only: Incorrect. This limits collection to only the West US workspace.

  • C. Analytics3 only: Incorrect. This is a common distractor on the AZ-104 exam. Candidates often mistakenly assume that because Vault1 is in West Europe, only a West Europe workspace (Analytics3) can be selected. While this same-region limitation applies if you were exporting to an Azure Storage Account, it does not restrict exports to Log Analytics workspaces.

You have an Azure virtual network named VNet1 that contains the following settings:

q297.explanation_html:
123 is the correct answer. The subnet 172.16.10.0/25 has a total of 128 IP addresses. However, Azure reserves the first four and the last IP address in every subnet for internal use. Therefore, the available IP addresses for virtual machines are:

128 (total IP addresses) – 5 (reserved addresses) = 123 usable IP addresses.

These 123 addresses can be assigned to virtual machines or other resources within the subnet.

172.16.10.0/25 means the subnet has 128 total IP addresses (2^7 = 128).

Azure reserves five IP addresses in each subnet:

  • The first IP is the network address.
  • The second through fourth IP addresses are reserved for Azure services.
  • The last IP address is reserved for the broadcast address.

Thus, 123 addresses remain available for virtual machines.

You have an Azure subscription that contains two peered virtual networks named VNet1 and VNet2. VNet1 has a VPN gateway that uses static routing,

The on-premises network has a VPN connection that uses the VPN gateway of VNet1.

You need to configure access for users on the on-premises network to connect to a virtual machine on VNet2. The solution must minimize costs.

Which type of connectivity should you use?
q304.explanation_html:
Service chaining and user-defined routes (UDRs) is the correct answer. By using service chaining and configuring user-defined routes (UDRs), you can route traffic from the on-premises network, through the VPN gateway on VNet1, to VNet2. This setup leverages the existing peering between VNet1 and VNet2 without requiring additional costly infrastructure like Azure Firewall or ExpressRoute, thereby minimizing costs. UDRs will ensure that the traffic is directed through the correct paths.

q305.question_html:

A backup vault and a Recovery Services vault are incorrect because they are used for backing up data and managing disaster recovery, not for rotating access keys.

Redundancy for storage1 is incorrect because it deals with the replication of storage data across different locations for high availability, not key management.

q311.explanation_html:
An internal load balancer is correct because an internal load balancer in Azure is designed to distribute network traffic within a virtual network (VNet) across virtual machines (VMs) without exposing them to the internet. In this scenario, it can be used to balance the load between the front-end web servers and the business logic tier, ensuring that traffic spreads equally across the VMs in the business logic tier. Since the business logic tier is not accessible from the internet, an internal load balancer is the appropriate solution.

An application gateway that uses the Standard tier is incorrect because an application gateway is primarily designed for web traffic (HTTP/HTTPS) and is typically used in internet-facing scenarios or for application layer load balancing, which is not specified here.

An application gateway that uses the WAF tier is incorrect for the same reason as above. Additionally, the WAF tier is designed to protect applications from web vulnerabilities, which is unnecessary for internal load balancing between tiers in this setup.

A network security group (NSG) is incorrect because NSGs are used for filtering network traffic based on security rules and do not provide load balancing capabilities.

A public load balancer is incorrect because it is used to distribute traffic from the internet to VMs within a VNet. Since the business logic tier is not accessible from the internet, a public load balancer is not suitable.

q312.explanation_html:

By placing an application gateway with WAF in front of the web servers, you can protect them from SQL injection and other security threats.

An application gateway that uses the Standard tier is incorrect because the Standard tier does not include WAF functionality, which is required to protect against SQL injection.

An internal load balancer is incorrect because load balancers are used to distribute network traffic and do not offer protection against SQL injection or other web vulnerabilities.

A network security group (NSG) is incorrect because NSGs control access through rules but do not provide protection against specific types of attacks like SQL injection.

A public load balancer is incorrect because, like an internal load balancer, it only distributes traffic and does not protect against web vulnerabilities.

You have an Azure Storage account named storage1 that contains a blob container named container1.

You need to prevent new content added to container1 from being modified for one year.

What should you configure?
q315.explanation_html:
An access policy is the correct answer because it allows you to configure immutability policies, such as time-based retention or legal hold, on a blob container. To prevent new content in the container from being modified for one year, you would set a time-based retention policy using a stored access policy that specifies the duration of the immutability period.

The Access control (IAM) settings is incorrect because IAM settings control role-based access to the storage account, not the immutability or modification rights of the data itself.

The access level is incorrect because this refers to the public access settings of the container, which determine if blobs are publicly accessible over the internet. It doesn‘t affect the ability to modify data within the container.

The access tier is incorrect because it defines the storage tier (Hot, Cool, or Archive) based on usage and access frequency, but it does not control modification or retention of content.
